sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Spring Security interview questions cover the auth layer that protects every modern Java backend — the SecurityFilterChain, authentication providers, password encoding, session vs stateless (JWT) auth, OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, method-level security (@PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize), CORS and CSRF, and the common pitfalls interviewers love to surface (storing JWTs in localStorage, missing audit fields, leaking principal in logs). This page covers Spring Security with Spring Boot 3, including the modern config-by-bean style and the migration patterns from the older WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter approach.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Spring Security is **a chain of filters**, then **method security** on top:

- **`SecurityFilterChain`** — request-level rules, AuthN, session strategy.
- **`AuthenticationManager`** + providers — DAO, LDAP, OAuth2, JWT.
- **Method security** — `@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`, SpEL.
- **Cross-cutting** — CORS, CSRF, headers, password encoders (`BCryptPasswordEncoder`).

Boot 3 / Security 6 dropped `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter`; everything is now bean-style.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Stateless JWT** — no server session, signature verification on every request; never put secrets in the JWT.
- **CSRF** — disable on stateless APIs only; keep enabled for cookie-session apps.
- **Password storage** — BCrypt (default), Argon2 if you can afford the cost.
- **Method security on `@Async`** — context propagation needs `DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable`.
- **OAuth2** — Resource Server vs Authorisation Server vs Client; name the role you're playing.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"I'd configure a `SecurityFilterChain` bean, route public/private paths explicitly, choose <JWT | session> based on <statelessness need>, encode passwords with BCrypt, and put method-level guards on the service. CSRF stays on for cookie auth, off for stateless JWT APIs."*
